text:
Hopefully someone else will chime in, but keep in mind that New Rochelle is in Westchester County just outside of NYC and the cost of living is higher than Upstate NY. So, less than $1200 a month will likely not get you too much.
If you are looking to come back to NY, you are going to have to look further north to find something decent/nicer with that rental budget.
Ironically, I'd say to look more mid Hudson Valley in the Poughkeepsie-Newburgh-Middletown area. You are more(key word) likely to find something within your budget and you still have commuter rail access into NYC from parts of that area. It is one of the most integrated metros in the country and has some of the smallest per capita income gaps between white residents and black, Hispanic, Asian residents in the country(if any gap at all). So, it can have some appeal as well. Places just outside of the cities such as Mechanicstown and Scothtown outside of Middletown; New Windsor, Orange Lake, Balmville and Garnertown outside of Newburgh; Arlington, Hyde Park and Spackenkill outisde of Poughkeepsie are diverse relatively middle class suburban communities. You also have walkable, bigger villages like Warwick, Goshen, Washingtonville, Wappingers Falls, Highland Falls, Monroe, Chester, Cornwall, etc. that nearby and have a decent mix of people as well in/near those communities.
If you don't mind looking further Upstate, select parts of the the metros and cities, as well as select towns may be a better fit. I'm thinking of more diverse suburban school districts like say South Colonie or North Colonie in the Albany area; Liverpool, Onondaga Central and Jamesville-Dewitt in the Syracuse area; maybe parts of the Johnson City and Union-Endicott SDs in the Binghamton area; Rush-Henrietta, Greece, East Irondequoit and Gates-Chili in the Rochester area and Sweet Home, Amherst Central, Cleveland Hill and Cheektowaga Central in the Buffalo area. All are solid to very good districts and with close proximity to the cities they are outside of. There are others that may work, but those are some places that come to mind that would be more likely to have something within your budget.

Since Connecticut is mentioned, overall the cost-of-living is high están Fairfield County (particularly on its coast) and gets loterías as you move into the other counties.
In terms of many other things Connecticut does tens to fall slightly higher than neighboring NY (particularly Westchester County, NYC and the counties in Long Island) and New Jersey. For example:
- When all taxes are paid, it will be less in Connecticut than in NY or NJ. In part because tax rates in general aren’t as high as in those states, but also because Connecticut doesn’t have as many taxes as they do in those states (and there are no county governments, so the taxes that usually comes with that simply doesn’t exist.)
- It has the 5th best highways in the nation surpassing NY/NJ and achieves that without tolls.
- Quality-of-life measured by HDI you’ll notice is basically the same or very similar at the state among all states in the country except with Massachusetts and Connecticut with these 2 being above.
- Outside the coastal areas of Fairfield County and the panhandle area traffic congestion/jams tend to be less both on local city/town streets and on the highways.
- Connecticut is centrally located between large cities such as NYC, Boston and Providence with easy access to all of them. So you can benefit with what they have to offer with not much difficulty by living in Connecticut.
- Winters in Connecticut are nowhere as bad (especially with the snow) as when you lived in Buffalo, NY. Even this winter where it has been colder than recent winters and has snowed more often, it still isn’t comparable with the area of Buffalo. Whatever memories (or nightmares, lol) you have of winters in Buffalo and made peace with the idea of returning to something similar to that, Connecticut is actually an improvement.
- I don’t know what part of Georgia you currently live in, though much of that state is flat. It will be a nice change that much of Connecticut is hilly and that means many nice views.
- All state parks ( including state beaches) and state forests are free of charge all year to Connecticut residents. If you like to hike and such even if once a while, that could be an added plus.
If you want a more detailed info on a certain area in Connecticut that might interest you as a place to live, consider asking that in the Connecticut forum. Quite a few people would help you with that.

New Rochelle will never be a "premier" suburb like Pelham/Larchmont/Mamaroneck/Scarsdale but it doesn't have to be. It could still be successful as a middle class commuter town -- cheaper than living in NYC and the commute to midtown isn't any longer from NewRo than it would be from lots of places in Queens or the Bronx or Hoboken. New Rochelle could be a good option for someone who works in the city but is priced out of Manhattan and prime Brooklyn. Also, there are some neighborhoods in NewRo with quite nice houses selling at a steep discount compared to the premier suburbs -- that could be an attractive trade-off for some people.
The schools in New Rochelle may not be on par with the premier suburbs, but that's not a fair comparison -- instead, you have to compare NR schools against schools in similarly priced neighborhoods in the outer boroughs, and NR schools are still a big improvement over many of those.
Most people reading this board can afford Scarsdale/Bronxville/Rye/Larchmont, and if you can afford those then you'll probably prefer those over New Rochelle...but that doesn't mean NR can't appeal to lots of people on a different budget.

I grew up in White Plains and live here now. I went through the school system and have two kids going through it now. I would not say White Plains is on the decline, but I would say it may have a bit of an identity crisis. It is definitely growing, and that is good or bad depending on who you ask. It was always a hybrid city-suburb, which is what we really like about it. There are neighborhoods that are as nice as Scarsdale or other wealthier towns, but also a city center where you can walk to restaurants, shops, train (40 min frequent express to NYC), etc. But the city seems to be intent on growing the downtown, mostly with high-rise luxury apartments. There was a city plan that hasn't been updated in 15 years and a lot of people, including myself, are confused as to where the city is going. We are not Yonkers, New Rochelle or Stamford, and I get the feeling that most residents like it this way, but the powers in charge are moving in that direction.
In any case, if you are worried about your property value, who knows what the future will bring, but things are definitely off the rails now. Not a good time to buy at all, properties go in days at above asking. But short answer, I don't think the city is in decline - it is growing, too fast, and with no clear direction. Take that how you want! :-)

text:
I lived in Astoria/Ditmars from '07-'08, then Forest Hills from '08-'12, then back in Astoria/Ditmars from '13-'14 before I had to leave NYC for work reasons. I would've gone back to Astoria sooner, but I bought a co-op in FH in 2008 right before the crash and wanted to stick around to see if the prices would recover. They never did and I ended up selling for a loss to move back.
FH is a nice enough neighborhood -- apartments are more "human sized" than Astoria and it's definitely prettier than Astoria if you overlook the Boulevard of Death. But I found it incredibly boring (and this is coming from someone who would probably be described by friends as incredibly boring ) The 71st Ave/Austin Street area is overrated and overrun with banks, pharmacies, and boutiques that I personally would never shop at (although others may feel differently). With some exceptions, the restaurants were generally mediocre and overpriced. One favorite feature, the Barnes and Noble, is long gone.
As has been mentioned, the scene in FH is definitely more family and elderly-oriented than Astoria. Granted, the Ditmars area is fairly subdued, but it's easy to get from Ditmars down to 30th Ave. or Broadway where there's a hotbed of activity in the evenings/weekends. In FH... not so much.
FH's transit options are outstanding with lots of buses, multiple subway lines and LIRR. I used to say the best thing about Forest Hills was the number of ways out! When I lived there, I spent a decent amount of time on Long Island and took the express bus to my job downtown, so the location was good for me. Don't be fooled though -- Astoria is significantly closer to the city than FH and even Jackson Heights. It's a long haul on the local trains and when there are delays (which are common). Jackson Heights and the Broadway area of Astoria are easily accessible by train, but it was a long enough trip that I didn't go that often. You may be more motivated.
Access to suburban-style shopping is good in the FH area, with easy access to Rego Center and the Queens Center Mall. That was something I missed in Astoria from time to time. I know you don't have a car, but for what it's worth, I think FH is a little more car friendly than the other areas -- street parking is horrendous in all of these places, but in FH there are at least options for paid parking, sometimes even in your own building.
Overall, you could certainly do worse than FH. Lots of folks would prefer it over the other areas you're thinking of which are comparatively ugly and noisy. Based on what you're looking for, I think you'd probably be happier in a livelier area if you could find a way to make that happen (living with roommates, etc.) Good luck!

Hi all!
I have been shopping for apartments and it looks like I've been temporarily priced out of my original top picks for neighborhoods in Western Queens (Jackson Heights and Ditmars/North Astoria). I'm now considering Forest Hills, since there's much more housing stock, and in terms of property, the bang/buck ratio seems much higher.
However, I have reservations about moving to FH given my current age and situation. Please respond with comments as I'm not sure all of my impressions are correct.
I work and go to grad school in Manhattan, and my friends are pretty dispersed around the city, though Manhattan usually ends up being our common meeting point due to proximity and the fact that most people are there anyway for work. Queens and northern BK friends (with cars, mostly) have expressed excitement about my potential move but other friends seem dubious about this decision and have expressed their reluctance to visit me in the boonies should I move there. This may seem trivial but as a single resident I do not want to set myself up for a lonely existence. FH people, do you have vibrant social lives both within and outside of the nabe, or are you too geographically limited to maintain such a lifestyle?
First of all, let it be known that I know that FH is, by common metrics, a "good neighborhood". It is incredibly safe, good schools, access to transit, relatively high average incomes, etc. However, I have seen a lot of nonsense on this forum especially from xenophobic racists who use coded language to prop up FH as essentially a whiter, and therefore better, option for Queens living. I don't really want to hear such foolishness on this thread.
FH seems pretty well served by trains (I have no car) but the units I am looking at are all surrounded by similarly boring residential towers. It's a pretty monotonous, if not excessively long, walk to the express train, and not past stores or a lively street There is very little street-level activity or commerce unless one walks to the Blvd or to Austin Street, which seem to be the only commonly-cited commercial streets around and which don't thrill me. Jackson Heights is remarkable in this regard, and I'm worried that the monotony of the layout (and the austerity of Queens Blvd) will prove exhausting.
Other neighborhoods seem to have better food/cafe options. JH has been my favorite food destination in NYC for years due to the intersection of cheapness/diversity/casual settings/overall authenticity, and it's difficult to take people seriously when they cite a single pizzeria and some run-of-the-mill pubs as evidence of FH's culinary richness. I don't care about "hipness" - I am, after all, searching in central Queens - but I do care about realness and quality. I am fine with traveling a bit to access bars/nightlife/etc since it's a once or twice a week phenomenon (if that) and I'd likely be meeting other non-Queens people on weekends. I do, however, care about access to good food on weekdays; I cook frequently but also frequently have long days where cheap eats are ideal. Anybody know of any worthwhile food spots in FH, or is it typical to leave the neighborhood for eating out? It's only ~10m to Jackson Hts. by train from FH but I wonder if people actually hop on a 7 or F just to get takeout on a wednesday night. Also, everyone always talks about how great shopping is around QB and Austin but I find most of the commerce there to be banking, women's clothing stores, and a multiplicity of Dunkin Donuts.
I hate to make this all sound like a complaint. I've found myself in and around the FH area at times throughout my life and it is admittedly scenic, quite green, the air tastes good for NYC standards, there is rarely if ever garbage in the streets, and I feel incredibly safe there and know that the stats back up this feeling. I also know that while the amenities here feel limited when compared with JH and Ditmars, they're pretty great compared to most other American cities, and even compared to many neighborhoods in Eastern Queens. However, I do have my concerns, as listed above, and I'd love to hear what people think. I know it is unfair to compare FH to JH or Ditmars in areas such as food, liveliness, diversity, etc. but I am trying to glean whether or not it has enough to offer in comparison. I'm not quite looking to move to the suburbs at this age, and FH sometimes feels like that kind of move. But I could be wrong. I'd love to hear all of your inputs as this is a big decision! Thanks!
